# 2 Maccabees Chapter 6 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_006_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Not long after this the king sent an old Athenian to compel the Jews to forsake the laws of their fathers and no longer to live by the laws of God,

**2** and also to pollute the temple in Jerusalem and to call it the temple of Olympian Zeus, and the one in Gerizim to be called the temple of Zeus-the-Friend-of-Strangers, as the inhabitants of that place indeed were.

**3** Harsh and utterly grievous was the onset of evil.

**4** For the temple was filled with debauchery and reveling by the Gentiles, who dallied with prostitutes and had intercourse with women within the sacred precincts, and besides brought in things for sacrifice that were not lawful.

**5** The altar was covered with abominable offerings that were forbidden by the laws.

**6** It was not possible to observe the sabbath or to celebrate the ancestral festivals, or even simply to acknowledge oneself to be a Jew.

**7** On the monthly birthday of the king, the Jews were driven by bitter constraint to partake of the sacrifices; and when the festival of Dionysus came, they were compelled to walk in the procession in honor of Dionysus, wearing wreaths of ivy.

**8** At the suggestion of Ptolemy a decree went out to the neighboring Greek cities that they should adopt the same policy toward the Jews and make them partake of the sacrifices,

**9** and that they should slay those who refused to change over to Greek customs. So the occasion of the present misery was plainly to be seen.

**10** For two women were brought in for having circumcised their children. These women were paraded about the city with their babies hanging at their breasts, then hurled down headlong from the wall.

**11** Others who had gathered in the caves nearby to observe the seventh day secretly were informed upon and burned together, because in their piety they had refused to defend themselves, out of respect for the holiness of that day.

**12** Now I urge those who read this book not to be depressed by such calamities, but to recognize that these punishments were designed not to destroy but to discipline our people.

**13** For it is a sign of great kindness not to let the impious alone for long but to punish them immediately.

**14** For in the case of the other nations the Sovereign Lord waits patiently until they have reached the full measure of their sins before punishing them, but in our case he has decided differently,

**15** in order that he may not take vengeance on us afterward when our sins have reached their height.

**16** Therefore he never withdraws his mercy from us. Though he disciplines us with calamities, he does not forsake his own people.

**17** Let what we have said be enough by way of reminder; after a few words we must get on with the account.

**18** Eleazar, one of the leading scribes, a man already advanced in years and of noble presence, was being forced to open his mouth and eat pork.

**19** But he, welcoming death with honor rather than life with pollution, went up to the rack of his own accord, spitting out the meat,

**20** as men ought to go who have the courage to refuse things that it is not right to taste, even for the natural love of life.

**21** Those who were in charge of that unlawful sacrifice, taking the man aside because of their long acquaintance with him, privately urged him to bring meat of his own providing, proper for him to use, and pretend that he was eating the flesh of the sacrificial meal which had been commanded by the king,

**22** so that by doing this he would be delivered from death, and for the sake of their old friendship with him they would be treating him kindly.

**23** But making a high resolve, worthy of his years and the dignity of his old age and the gray hairs which he had reached with such distinction and his excellent life even from childhood, and moreover according to the holy God-given law, he declared himself quickly, telling them to send him to Hades.

**24** "Such pretense is not worthy of our time of life," he said, "lest many of the young should suppose that Eleazar in his ninetieth year has gone over to an alien religion,

**25** and through my pretense and for the sake of living this brief moment longer I become a cause of defilement and a stain upon my old age.

**26** Even if for the present time I avoid the punishment of men, yet whether I live or die I shall not escape the hands of the Almighty.

**27** Therefore, by bravely giving up my life now, I will show myself worthy of my old age,

**28** and leave to the young a noble example of how to die a good death willingly and nobly for the revered and holy laws."

**29** When he had said this, he went at once to the rack.

**30** And those who a little before had been acting with goodwill now changed to ill will, because the words he had uttered were in their opinion sheer madness.

**31** When he was about to die from the blows, he groaned aloud and said: "It is clear to the LORD in his holy knowledge that, though I might have been saved from death, I am enduring terrible agonies in my body under this beating, but in my soul I am glad to suffer these things because I fear him."

**32** So in this way he died, leaving in his death an example of nobility and a memorial of virtue not only to young men but to the whole nation.
